newsitem.title: USA: Dlr losses mount at US noon, hits 3-mth low vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr losses mount at US noon, hits 3-mth low vs yen.

text.p: The dollar crumbled during U.S. morning trade, hitting its lowest point against the yen since January 27, triggering numerous stop-loss orders and a broad-based pullout from long dollar positions, dealers said.

Shortly before 1200 EDT/1600 GMT the dollar began a sudden two-yen decline to 119 as technical supports including a major floor at 120 gave way. The greenback just as suddenly regained 120, but then settled below that level in early afternoon.
"We seemed to find some support as we approached 120, but it's been pretty wild," said one trader. "Obviously as we move lower, the stop-loss levels become more and more important."

The dollar traded at 120.20/25 yen at midday, down from 121.95/00 at the open and 123.75/80 at Thursday's close. Against the mark, the dollar fell to 1.6863/68 from 1.6995/00 at the open and 1.7075/85 at Thursday's close.
Dealers cited a reversal in expectations for official U.S. and Japanese interest rates as well as repeated jawboning by Japanese officials for deflating the dollar.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Thursday night speech was seen by many market players as a signal that Fed policymakers will not raise rates at their May 20 meeting. Meanwhile, Japanese Government bond yields rose sharply.

"The market is worried about a (Bank of Japan) tightening at the same time it's having second thoughts about the Fed tightening," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The dollar's spectacular swoon of nearly eight yen in the past week has frightened away even the most ardent dollar bulls, traders said.
The prospect of further panic selling has bottom-fishers reeling in their lines, and short-term speculators drooling.
"I don't think this is the environment for trying to pick a bottom for the dollar," said Chandler.
The yen also surged against the mark, slashing the mark/yen cross a full yen to the 71.40 area, its lowest reading in two months.
"With the amount that's been sold in mark/yen it's amazing how well it was holding," said Edith Wolf, a vice president for foreign exchange sales at Credit Commerciale de France.

But the mark enjoyed continuing strength versus the British pound, with sterling/mark falling nearly four pfennigs from its session high to below 2.74. The Swiss franc also gained on residual expectations that Europe's proposed single currency might include sterling in a wide-reaching membership.
Some dealers lamented that the Swiss, mark and yen buying reflected more hysteria than an accurate fundamental view.
"I think the deutschemark is way too rich and I think the Swiss is a joke up here," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
Still, few market players could muster the courage to buy the dollar on supportive long-term fundamentals in the face of dangerous short-term gyrations.
"You're just getting people throwing in the towel. The yen is dragging everything with it and funds are forced to cover," Malpede said.

Greenspan overnight defended the Fed's modest rate hike on March 25, asserting the central bank would act again if the economy failed to slow. But he conceded he saw little evidence of resurgent U.S. inflation.

The dollar fell to 1.4225/35 Swiss francs from 1.4350/60 at the open and 1.4455/65 at Thursday's close. Sterling was flat at $1.6205/15. The greenback rost to Canadian $1.3901/06 from C$1.3840/45 at the open.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
